# Copper November 2012 - Copper prices moved lower over the first couple of weeks of November, as the US elections and the leadership change in China weighed on the markets. At the same time exchange stocks continued to pile higher and add further downward pressure to an already bearish market. Copper prices have since staged a slow recovery since hitting the low of $7506 (3-month) on 9th November with the prompt being positive economic news from China rather than anything of a fundamental nature. The industry has convened in China for the first Asia Copper Week, where premia for 2013 cathode contracts are under discussion. The prevailing economic uncertainty seems to have favoured consumers as premia touted so far are lower than those quoted for 2012. - The key themes which keep coming through in our analysis of downstream demand are restructuring and substitution. Semis producers in the traditional demand centres are battling to remain in business as they are buffeted by tough financing conditions, sluggish economic activity and in many cases low cost competition from abroad. This would be bad enough but copper continues to come under threat from substitution. Many in the industry will be relieved when the year is over as we forecast demand will grow by 5.1% next year compared to the muted 1.2% expansion in 2012. Significantly, the main change from last month was a downgrade to Chinese consumption growth from 6.25% previously to 5% now. - With spot market activity remaining sporadic, selling terms continued their gradual upward movement of recent months, with $66/t and 6.6c/lb being a representative average of levels achieved between miners and traders. Further meetings between Freeport and Japanese smelters to negotiate long-term benchmark TC/RCs for 2013 are rumoured to have taken place during the month, although little progress has been reported. BHPBilliton, acting on behalf of Escondida, is thought to have adopted an aggressive attitude in its negotiations with Chinese smelters, offering 12 month deals with TC/RCs in the region of $60/t & 6.0c/lb. There have been suggestions that the Chilean miner is seeking premium terms to reflect the anticipated supply of higher grade concentrates next year. #### **Copper key forecasts** ||**2011**|**%**|**2012**|**%**|**2013**|**%**|**2014**|**%**| |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| |**Global (kt)**||||||||| |Total Mine Production|16129|-0.3|16729|3.7|18018|7.7|19487|8.2| |Total Smelter Production|15425|4.3|15746|2.1|16979|7.8|18084|6.5| |Refined Production|19660|3.6|20113|2.3|21387|6.3|22888|7.0| |Consumption|19711|2.2|19956|1.2|20971|5.1|22136|5.6| |Concentrate Market Balance|-353||0||50||100|| |Metal Market Balance|-51||157||416||753|| |Metal Stocks-Days of Cons|57||59||63||72|| |**Prices**||||||||| |Cash LME Price ($/t)|8810||7946||7725||7238|| |(c/lb)|400||360||350||328|| |Contract TC/

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

Copper prices moved lower over the first couple of weeks of November, as the US elections and the leadership change in China weighed on the markets.  At the same time exchange stocks continued to pile higher and add further downward pressure to an already bearish market. 

The market tumbled to a low of $7506/t in early November after the Dow registered its biggest one day loss in 2012 in a post-election sell off that was further aggravated by Mario Draghi’s comments that Euro Zone debts and their problems were now starting to affect the German economy.  Meanwhile in China, the country’s Communist party began its 18th Congress in Beijing.  Now that the US election is over and the Chinese leadership change has taken place, the focus has once again shifted to the trio of the US fiscal cliff, the Chinese economy and European debt.  These (either collectively or distinctly) will remain the key background influences behind the macro economic sentiment that will drive copper price movements. 

**China props up prices…** Copper prices have staged a slow recovery since hitting the low of $7506 (3-month) on 9<sup>th</sup> November with the prompt economic rather than fundamental.  Positive news from China that the trade surplus rose by the largest amount in nearly four years to $32Bn, as exports increased by 11.6% in October, beating expectations, helped push 3-month prices closer to the $7700/t level.  However, subsequent news that the Euro zone had slipped into its second recession since 2009 saw copper dip lower again as did the preliminary data that imports of copper into China were much lower on a month-on-month basis.  Since mid-November, however, copper prices have staged a much healthier recovery with 3-month quotes breaching the $7700/t level, backed by the positive macro economic data that has come out of China recently.  Indeed it was the positive tone of the HSBC’s flash estimate of the manufacturing purchasing managers’ index that sparked the recovery.  The Flash PMI rose from 49.5 to reach a 13-month high of 50.4 in November.  This was the first reading above the ‘break-even’ level of 50 since October 2011 and the up-tick was driven mainly by a rebound in the output component to 51.3 from 48.2 in October, the biggest monthly rise this year.  The data suggests that conditions in China’s economy have stabilised and the unyielding machine that is China has begun to improve, albeit at a very slow pace.  PMI Inventories continued to show a decline, but at a slower pace (the inventories index rose from 48.4 to 49.5, while new orders also cooled (down from 51.2 to 50.1).  On a more positive note however, new export orders surged from 46.7 to 52.4, their largest monthly rise since April 2009.

**… amid signs that copper demand is returning** On the ground and despite the ongoing build in SHFE inventories, which have increased steadily since June and rose 13kt over the past month, there are encouraging signs that demand for copper has improved slightly since November. Demand is slowly benefitting from the some of the stimulus polices which were announced back in September while destocking across the manufacturing chain appears to be almost at an end. Moreover, a recent announcement that the Chinese government has approved construction of two city subway projects worth 49 billion Yuan (£4.91 billion), in addition to the list of recent railway projects approved back in September which totalled $157Bn, should go some way to boosting demand growth from 2013. All these projects should help to prop up growth in China's economy, which has slowed for seven consecutive quarters, and most recently posted annual growth of 7.4% in the third quarter. Recent data shows that the economy has turned a corner with fixed-asset investment, factory output, and retail sales all beating expectations in October. In addition, the Ministry of Railways announced it had raised its spending plan for 2013 to 630Bn Yuan from the 610Bn Yuan announced in September. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2012 Page 2 of 21 Copper Monthly Update The Chinese copper sector data is also more positive. Copper semis production continues to rise, up 10.7% in the year to October and we understand that orders for semi manufactured products are steadily improving month on month. Wire rod demand improved through November on the back of an uptick in orders from the power cable and magnet wire sectors. Meanwhile, power cable output has grown 12.9% in the year to October and rose by 10.7% year on year in October. The wire rod sector will benefit from the ongoing investment in the power grid, which should feed into investment into the copper intensive power generation sector. Although demand has yet to improve from the construction sector, floor space under construction rose 15.4% in October, with residential construction up 10.6%. While a better indicator for copper demand is home completions, as copper wire is consumed at the end of the construction process, the overall improvement in the sector bodes well for copper once these construction projects are finished in the spring, given that the cold weather has already started to impact some of these projects, particularly in northern China. Copper tube demand has remained subdued. As expected, production of air-conditioners fell in October, down 6.0% month-on-month, and largely reflected the Chinese holiday at the beginning of Octobe

r. Given the build in inventory that the industry experienced earlier this year, producers are reluctant to ramp up their production in the absence of any clear indications of a robust upturn, even though production should theoretically improve through November in preparation of the seasonal uptick in exports in the Spring. Demand for flat rolled products is mixed with strong growth only in the highend sector. **Semis capacity continues to build** In the meantime, rod projects continue to be approved. Baosheng Cable, a cable producer recently announced its plans for a 300kt/a SCR wire rod line and comes on the back of Guangxi Jinhong Metal’s 200kt/a bright copper rod project and Tongling’s order of a 225kt/a Contirod wire rod line with commissioning slated for the second half of 2013. These are in addition to a huge slew of wire rod projects that have already been announced and ties up with our understanding that Chinese semis capacity and production is increasing at the expense of imported semis. #### **Chinese imports of semis and wire and cable – (kt copper weight)** 1500

China has slowly been shifting its focus to domestic production of semi manufactured products with the expansion of semis capacity and in particular cathode intensive rod capacity. This shift has been mirrored by developments on the supply side with copper smelting and refined capacity increasing a pace over the past few years. China now accounts for around 25-30% of global refined production and this is set to rise to potentially 37% by 2015. So it is no surprise that reports are filtering through that the Chinese cathode import requirements could ease in 2013. Of course that presupposes that the Chinese smelters are able to obtain all the copper raw material feed that they need to produce an impressive ~7Mt of copper cathode at full capacity (and before any market adjustments are applied). We believe this to be highly unlikely. The record of disruptions to the mines of the past few years has meant that smelters and refiners have not been able to produce close to optimum capacity levels as they have not been able to source sufficient concentrate. This has led to an increase in scrap consumed by the smelters in an attempt to maintain production levels in the face of both constrained concentrate availability as well as lower grade concentrate. These factors combined have capped refined production growth in China and even though we are forecasting an uplift in concentrate output for 2013, it is unlikely that the Chinese smelters will be able to source all the raw material that they would ideally like, thus constraining cathode output to around 6.3Mt. Add to the mix a significant build in cathode inventory of around 500-600kt throughout this year,

Of course this assumes that the producers and consumers who have convened at the first Asia Copper Week (ACW), now the third leg of the mating season which kicked off in London during LME week and was swiftly followed by the American Copper Council’s (ACC) Fall Meeting in mid-November, will come to an agreement over terms and volumes for 2013 copper cathode contracts. Premia have been the main focus of debate thus far with reports that Chinese consumers will be paying anything from $93 to $100/t for their long-term tonnages. As highlighted in the section on Concentrate Markets, concentrate negotiations will also be taking place. These follow a series of meetings in the calendar that have already taken place in Europe and Japan since LME week with further discussions likely in the next few weeks if nothing is confirmed during ACW. **Surplus to emerge as demand outlook softens** It is clear, however, that negotiations across the copper chain will be difficult. The refined market is expected to register a surplus of ~400kt next year, pushing stocks to 63 days of consumption from around 56 currently. At one end of the spectrum, the end users have no clarity to their order books given these uncertain economic climes. So as negotiations take place at the various stages of the chain it comes as no surprise to hear reports that cathode consumers are looking to either maintain volumes at the same level as their 2012 contracts or even reduce them in some instances. We have also heard some reports that due to the weakness in demand this year, there will be some overhang of deliveries into 2013, with the result that some cathode contracts are only likely to start from February/March 2013. #### **Copper spot premia – ($/t)** 180 10

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2012 Page 4 of 21 Copper Monthly Update Meanwhile spot interest has faded away as consumers look to reduce inventories ahead of the year-end break. As a result, premia have not changed from the levels quoted

last month in Europe and the USA. In China, however, the combination of an uptick in order activity as well as an improved arbitrage during November saw the premium for imported cathode increase slightly and have been quoted in a range of $40-70/t compared to levels of $30-60/t last month. This is despite rising inventories at SHFE and bonded warehouse inventories of around 770kt, somewhat lower than the extravagant 1Mt levels that have been reported in the press recently. **Prices continue to track the macro but fundamentals will still play their role** As we look ahead prices will continue to be swayed by the trio of the US Fiscal Cliff, China and Europe. Indeed the market reacted positively to the aid deal for Greece at the start of this week, helping to nudge 3-month prices closer to the $7800/t level, while positive comments out of the USA, suggesting some resolution over the issue of its Fiscal Cliff helped 3-month copper breach the $7800/t barrier. However as we go to press, the news that unions at the Chuquicamata, Radomiro Tomic and Gaby mines have blocked access and prevented the 7am shift changeover (Chilean Time) has pushed prices even higher to breach the $7900/t mark. This action is part of the labour negotiations that have been ongoing since 11th November and are expected to continue until mid-December 2012. One of the key bones of contention is the plan put forward by the management at Chuquicamata to dismiss over 2,000 workers over the next four years. Discussions are also taking place in Zambia that could yet affect output at Glencore’s Mopani copper operations, Vedanta’s Konkola Copper Mines unit, Jinchuan Group’s Chibuluma mine and CNMC’s Luanshya mine, who are demanding pay increases of as much as 50% for 2013. The markets will focus in the short term on the outcome of the discussions in Chile which will provide support to the price while European concerns and the shaky Chinese demand outlook are likely to temper any significant rallies. Our average price forecast for this year is (as might be expected by November) little changed at $7946/t ($3.60/lb). For 2013 we have lowered our estimate moderately to $7725/t ($3.50/lb) in tandem with a somewhat weaker demand forecast. For the following year, a combination of higher refined production under a scenario of slower demand growth has resulted in our lowering our price projection to $7238/t ($3.28/lb) in 2014. #### **Price forecasts and world quarterly supply/demand balance – (kt)** |||**Refined**

## Consumption 

The key themes which keep coming through in our analysis of downstream demand are restructuring and substitution. Semis producers in the traditional demand centres are battling to remain in business as they are buffeted by tough financing conditions, sluggish economic activity and in many cases low cost competition from abroad.  This would be bad enough but copper continues to come under threat from substitution.  Many in the industry will be relieved when the year is over as we forecast demand will grow by 5.1% next year compared to the muted 1.2% expansion in 2012. Significantly, the main change from last month was a downgrade to Chinese consumption growth from 6.25% previously to 5% now and we discuss this in more detail next month. 

### **Germany** 

**Varying degrees of success** The degree to which semis producers have suffered in Germany this year has varied, with some mills reporting a more severe downturn than others, although the recent trend of stabilisation appears to be consistent across all firms.  The bad news is that this is being reported at low levels.  Our view is that some mills have lost market share to other regional producers and we expand upon this in more detail below.  Significantly, “stabilisation” will still represent modest year-on-year growth in fourth quarter cathode demand due to the extremely weak end to 2011. 

**Comparative advantage lies in wire and cable** Analysis of trade figures reveals a great deal about the comparative advantage in the downstream copper industry in Germany.  Grouping product lines into rod/wire, brass mill and wire and cable, it is rod/wire exports that have performed the worst, while wire and cable was the best of the three despite a year to date decline of 3.8% through August.  Given that wire rod is a commodity product, purchasing decisions tend to centre on price and in an economic downturn the cost to consumers becomes of particular importance.  We understand that German mills have lost share to European neighbours as a result of competitors offering more attractive overall pricing and payment terms.  However, German companies would appear to have a comparative advantage in wire and cable where for particular applications quality and reliability are more importan

t than a small relative price difference. 

**Autos move into slow lane** Automotive has been one of the strongest sectors in Germany this year, where demand has remained robust despite declining car output.  The underlying strength is a function of the higher average copper content of premium marques which have enjoyed steady production as a result of relatively robust export growth.  Up until recently this had resulted in sectoral demand remaining healthy, although over the past few months consumption has begun to wane as car production hit the brakes, leading German wiring harness supplier Leoni to downgrade its Q4 sales forecast.  Car output is forecast to turn higher again in 2013 buoyed by modest improvements in export markets which should support demand for items such as wiring harnesses. 

**Lack of spark in other sectors** Other sectors have been mixed in their performance this year with construction better than in Southern European countries but not by much, while in electrical infrastructure government delays on spending are impeding much needed investment.  In particular, some offshore wind energy projects are on hold because of concern that they will not be connected to the mainland grid.  There is a need for investment in Germany, in particular between the North and the South but in current austere times major projects are stalled.  Meanwhile, copper’s use in power cables continues to be pressured by substitution from aluminium. 

**Modest upturn in 2013 after c.9% decline this year** The broadly negative backdrop and sharp slowdown in demand from the automotive sector have confirmed our bearish stance on German consumption and we reiterate our estimate of a 9.1% decline this year.  For 2013 we forecast a modest recovery in demand of around 2-3% as destocking through the supply chain is replaced by a mild restock, in line with stabilising European economic activity. 

### **Italy** 

**Semis production bucks down trend** The most positive news to emerge from Italy for some time came in the form of the latest semis production data, which revealed that output rose for the first time since the first quarter of 2011. Production of copper alloys boosted the third quarter total, rising by 15.7% year on year to 123kt, buoyed by strong gains in output of bars and sections.  Copper semis output in Q3 was up by a more sedentary 1.1% on the same period a year ago at 124.9kt to result in total semis production rising by 7.8% overall to 247.9kt. 

**Substitution eats in to demand at the margin** The semis output data does hint at substitution of copper given the much stronger rise in alloy products relative to pure copper semis.  This has also been confirmed in our discussions with market participants who explained that firms have been either increasing the overall proportion of alloys or introducing new alloys where previously the product would have been pure copper.  The key point here is that substitution does not just manifest itself in swit

ching from copper to aluminium, for example, but changing the composition of alloys can also be significant. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2012 Page 6 of 21 Copper Monthly Update #### **Italian semis production – (kt)** 40 360

**Exports of semis support refined demand** Without doubt underlying demand for copper products is weak in Italy and this is reflected in the sluggish state of imports of semis. In the face of a weak domestic market, Italian semis producers have at least had some success exporting overseas, although not all parts of the value chain have been effective in doing this. For example, exports of wire rod are up by 47% to 53.1kt in the first eight months of the year, although exports of wire and cable are down by 5% over the same period. Given that imports of semis are down and exports are higher, underlying demand for semis has been much worse in Italy than demand for cathode. As a result, downstream businesses continue to investigate opportunities for cutting costs and streamlining operations in order to maintain competitiveness. **Automotive sector in the headlights** The construction market is a focus for demand weakness across Europe but there are few places where demand is as sluggish as Italy. Both the residential and non residential sectors remain mired in problems and continue to contract, with 2013 forecast to decline further still. Consumer products, such as white goods are suffering from the slow pace of activity in construction, while the generally downbeat tone to economic conditions is leading to a reluctance in firms to invest and as a result the industrial segment is also flagging. However, the automotive market is proving to be a beacon of hope, with car production estimated to rise by some 20% in Italy this year, with a similar gain forecast for 2013. **2012 refined demand estimate upgraded** Stronger than anticipated production in the third quarter is largely responsible for an upgrade to our estimate of refined consumption in 2012 and we now expect a full year contraction of only around 2% this year. ### **Japan** **Firms fighting to remain competitive** There have been further announcements of restructuring and integration in Japan this month as semis producers and downstream consumers seek to improve their competitiveness. Firstly, Sumitomo Metal Mining and Hitachi Cable are to integrate their lead frame and copper products businesses, although Hitachi’s tube and brass products segment will be excluded from the deal. Under the agreement, Hitachi Cable will supply copper strip for lead frame applications while SMM’s expertise in overseas marketing is hoped

to generate synergies and increase overall sales.  The new ventures, which will be integrated in April 2013, will also aim to increase sales to the automotive and industrial sectors.  Meanwhile, Furukawa Electric has announced that it is to restructure its copper wire rod 0and wire and cable business.  The release stated that it is to pull out of some winding wire product lines owing to their low profitability, while at the same time it will transfer production overseas of some industrial wire in addition to copper foil.  There will also be administrative cut backs with the aim of increasing operating profits.  Our long term forecasts for refined demand in Japan are for continued contraction, based on the premise that domestic firms such as Furukawa Electric will gradually move production of low value added products off-shore.  This trend of off-shoring production is not specific to the copper sector but has been a feature of Japanese industry in general for the past two decades.  The net result is a contracting industrial base and as a consequence demand for refined copper in Japan has been on a downward spiral since the early 1990s. 

**Sluggish exports weigh on domestic refined demand** While in Italy we revealed that underlying demand is actually worse than cathode consumption, in Japan the reverse is true.  Although semis production has, on the whole, disappointed this year, it has been the weakness in exports of semis that has dragged output lower.  Shipments of wire

and cable illustrate this trend, with total shipments up a respectable 2.3% in the first ten months of the year overall, despite exports slumping by 25.5% year-to-date.  The brass mill sector shows a similar, yet more bearish trend, with production declining by 7.7% over January to September but exports sliding by 15.9% over the same period.  Stripping out exports would reveal a healthier picture for domestic brass mill demand. 

**Imports washing up onshore** Wire and cable imports reveal another striking trend that reinforces our point about offshoring.  So far this year wire and cable imports have risen by 13.5% but more staggering is the increase in inbound shipments of automotive wiring harnesses, which have surged by 35%.  Over recent decades Japanese companies have set up a number of overseas subsidiaries in ASEAN countries, including but not exclusively for the assembly of wiring harnesses.  Yazaki is the latest company to do so, opening its first plant in Cambodia just recently.  This is partly behind the strength in demand in these countries to date but also why we are bullish on their outlook, in stark contrast to our longer term projections for Japan. 

**Autos set to move down a gear** The sharp increase in wiring harness imports into Japan also underlines the strength in demand of the automotive sector.  In the first nine months of this year car output has risen by 34

% on a combination of favourable base effects and demand being boosted by sales incentive schemes. This has resulted in shipments of wire and cable to the automotive sector climbing by 25% in the January to October period, while brass mill shipments show a similar trend. Automotive has been the stand out sector in Japan so far this year, which is why it is a concern that the production of vehicles and demand from this sector is beginning to wane. Despite the impressive year to date figures, car production fell by 12.5% year on year in September, while latest figures reveal a 6.7% year-on-year fall in registrations in October, after car purchase incentive schemes came to an end. This indicates a period of weakness in the road ahead for the sector, with negative year-on-year growth in car production expected to persist well into next year. **Construction builds momentum…** Another sector that has done relatively well this year has been construction, which is enjoying a mild upturn in the aftermath of last year’s earthquake and tsunami. Wire and cable shipments to the sector are up by 3.3% in the first ten months of the year, buoyed by rebuilding efforts which looks set to continue to boost demand given the improvement in housing starts that has taken place through the year. **…but weakness elsewhere forces FY downgrade** Other sectors are faring less well. Investment in electrical infrastructure remains squeezed as energy firms switch spending to expensive imports of fossil fuels and this has resulted in a 12.5% contraction in power cable shipments through the first ten months of the year. Telecom and electrical machinery shipments are not progressing as badly but are still well down on last year. It is with this in mind, in addition to the particular weakness of brass mill shipments, that we have been forced to tone down our demand projection and we now estimate no growth at all this year followed by only a modest expansion in 2013. ### **Thailand** **Sequential recovery from last year’s floods** Thai copper consumption was on track for steady if unspectacular growth in 2011 until major floods hit economic activity in the final part of the year. This resulted in demand slowing sharply in the

fourth quarter, which ultimately led to a 5.5% full year contraction, although consumption has picked up steadily since then and is set to record growth of 7.1% in 2012. Metals Market Service Monthly Update - November 2012 Page 8 of 21 Copper Monthly Update **OEM component plants drive demand** Much of the growth in copper demand in Thailand over the past decade has stemmed from overseas investment by OEM component makers, with Japanese companies in particular at the forefront of this. When Japanese firms move overseas they often bring a supply chain with them and this, allied to the ultimate aim of lowering costs, is behind the moves of Furukawa, Yazaki and Kobelco among others. A good deal of this investment has focussed on the automotive industry but there has also been significant off-shoring to Thailand in air conditioner manufacture. Car production was not immune from the impact of the floods and total vehicle production declined by 10% last year but is rebounding strongly and is estimated to surge by some 41% in 2012 and a further 16% in 2013. This will continue to support strong growth in wiring harness assembly and thus demand for wire rod, which will be largely met by domestic production. **Improving external markets support 2013 outlook** Moving into 2013 we remain bullish on the outlook for demand in Thailand in part owing to expectations of further growth in the automotive sector but also because of improvement in export markets in general. Healthier external markets will lift domestic semis production and therefore refined demand. We remain bullish in the outlook further out not least because earlier this year Sumitomo Electric Industries announced plans to build a 120kt/a rod mill in Thailand. #### **Production and shipments of copper wire rod and copper semis – (kt)** ||**2009**|**2010**|**2011**|**2011**

**Upward trend for Chinese concentrate imports continues** Despite the fact that there were 8 days of national holidays during October, Chinese copper concentrate imports continued to rise as smelters, encouraged by the improving arbitrage between the SHFE and LME copper prices and higher TCRCs, sought to replenish low inventories. October’s figure of 716kt was marginally higher than September’s import figure of 704kt and took the year to date total to 6.06Mt, 18% higher than the equivalent period during 2011. 

**Daye refinery expansion** Daye Non Ferrous is understood to have started commissioning tests on new refining capacity rated at 300kt/a.  These new facilities are not expected to enter commercial production until local demand for refined copper improves, but at full capacity they will boost Daye’s output capability to 600kt/a of refined copper cathode. Daye’s existing Ausmelt unit is rated to handle 1.5Mt/a of concentrate.  Given the mismatch between smelter and refinery capacity, the company is believed to be studying options to increase its primary smelting capability, but until these plans are realised additional feed requirements for the new refining capacity will be met by sourcing blister/anode from third parties. 

**Kansanshi smelter approved** The Zambian Environmental Management Agency (ZEMA) has approved First Quantum Minerals’ plans to build a 300kt/a copper smelter at Kansanshi in the Zambian copper belt.  The $640M project is expected to enter production in 2014 and will process concentrates from First Quantum’s Kansanshi mine and the

**First shipment from Antapaccay** Xstrata has reported the start of production at its new Antapaccay mine in Peru and the delivery of the first shipment of copper concentrate to the port of Matarani for export. **Atlas to supply local smelter** Atlas Consolidated Mining and Development Corporation has announced the shipment of two 5kt parcels of concentrate to Philippines Associated Smelting and Refining Corp. (PASAR).  The mining operations of Atlas are located on Cebu Island in the Philippines and since re-opening in 2008 have shipped concentrates to Chinese and Korean smelters.  Production is forecast to increase from 33kt of copper in concentrate in 2011 to in excess of 40kt/a in 2012 and future years, reflecting the switch from mining the Lutopan deposit to the higher grade Carmen deposit in June of this year.  The PASAR smelter, located on the island of Leyte in the Philippines, is 78% owned by Glencore.  The deal with Atlas is believed to be the first for more than a decade that PASAR has sourced feed material from a local mine.  The PASAR smelter, which re-opened in July after a six month stoppage due to a fire is understood to be considering a $600M investment to increase throughput from 700kt/a to 1.2Mt/a of concentrate.

**Ronnskar maintenance** Boliden reported Q3 cathode production from its Ronnskar smelter and refinery complex of 49.1kt, down by 11% on the e

quivalent period in 2011.  The shortfall was attributed to disruptions during the restart of operations after a maintenance shutdown.  The amount of electronic scrap processed at the facility was also down on the previous quarter as more lead concentrate was processed through the smelter’s Kaldo furnaces.  These furnaces are a form of top blown rotary convertor suited to treating complex and potentially hazardous feed material as the vessel design allows different reaction steps to be executed in sequence whilst generating low off-gas flows.  At Ronnskar the Kaldo furnaces are used to treat either lead concentrates or electronic scrap on a campaign basis.  Meanwhile, Boliden gave notice of a ‘once in 25-year’ shutdown scheduled for Ronnskar in 2013.  It is understood that this is likely to start in May, although the expected duration is unconfirmed. 

## Blister/anode and scrap markets 

**More Chinese secondary capacity** Guangxi Non Ferrous Metals announced that its secondary smelter and refinery project at Wuzhou entered commercial production during November.  Although the facility is ultimately intended to produce 300kt/a of refined copper from a mixture of high and low grade scrap (including e-scrap) only 150kt/a of production capability has currently been commissioned.  Meanwhile, Tongling Non Ferrous is reported to be building a secondary smelting and refining facility at Zhangjiang.  Output from this facility is scheduled to reach 300kt/a of copper by 2013. 

**Chinese scrap imports slower** According to trade statistics, imports of copper scrap into China during October were 394kt taking the year to date total to 3.95Mt up by 3.6% on the equivalent period during 2011.  Tight supply and an ever increasing population of secondary smelters requiring feed material saw the average local discount for No.2 scrap narrow to 3000RMB/t (22c/lb) by mid November which was around 600RMB/t (4c/lb) lower than the start of the month.

**Spot blister market quiet** As in preceding months the spot blister market has been quiet with indicative Chinese spot terms standing at around $120/t.  On the basis of our expectation of higher smelter utilisation rates nex

t year, we anticipate that long-term blister RCs are likely to rise from the 2012 level of $88/t cif Europe to perhaps $120-$130/t for 2013. 

**Russian copper rod from scrap project** A EUR50M project to produce copper rod from scrap in the Tula region of Russia has been announced.  The plant will be constructed by a joint venture between the La Farga Group of Spain and Russia’s RUSSKAT and is scheduled to come into operation in 2014 and produce 20kt/a of rod. 

**Japanese smelters consume more alloy scrap** According to statistics released by the Japanese Ministry of Economy, Trade & Industry, consumption of copper alloy scrap by the country’s smelters in September totalled 35.7kt, 91% higher than the same month in 2011, representing the 8<sup>th</sup> consecutive month of year-on-year gains.  With concentrate TCRCs still relatively low, and mine supply proving unreliable due to disruptions, Japanese smelters have been increasingly looking to boost their profitability by recovering copper and precious metals from secondary material.  Treating scrap also allows smelters to maintain production levels despite falling concentrate grades.  In addition to alloy scrap, secondary feed sources for Japanese smelters include shredder dust, fly ash and industrial waste.  Japanese imports of copper scrap for the year to September totalled 105kt, 4% lower than for the equivalent period during 2011, implying that the extra scrap consumed during 2012 has been from domestic sources.  However, with low levels of industrial and building activity the supply of scrap in Japan is understood to be tight. 

## Production news 

**Mixed performance from Codelco divisions** Reported commercial production from Chilean state owned copper miner, Codelco for the first nine months of 2012 totalled 1188kt, 95% of the output achieved during the equivalent period in 2011.  Combined production from the Chuquicamata and Radomirio Tomic operations in the north of the country, where output has been hampered by falling ore grades and smelter downtime, totalled 562kt over the nine months compared to 678kt in the same period in 2011.  This shortfall was partially mitigated by improved performance at the company’s other mines.  At El Teniente, where output was impacted by industrial action from contract workers during 2011, production of 305kt in the first nine months of the year was 13% higher than in 2011.  Andina, which is benefitting from improved throughput as a mill expansion to 94kt/d ramps up to full capacity, achieved 182kt in the first nine months of 2012, a 7% increase on the 2011 figure.  Meanwhile output at the Minera Gaby leach/SxEw operation, which was adversely affected by crusher problems in 2011, was 96kt in the first nine months of 2012, up by 14% on levels last year.  The Ministro Mina Hales (MMH) project, rated to produce up to 215kt/a of copper in concentrate, is reported to be still on target for commissioning during 2013, although estimates of the total capital

investment required for the project have now risen to $3.5Bn compared to $2.3Bn when construction commenced in 2011. 

**Esperanza ramp up boosts Antofagasta** Antofagasta PLC reported copper production for the first nine months of the year of 516kt, an 11.5% increase on the equivalent period in 2011.  Output was boosted by the ongoing ramp up of production at the Esperanza mine in northern Chile that started operations in January 2011.  Year to date production of payable copper in concentrate totalled 114kt compared to 54kt during the first nine months of 2011.  Ore throughput during the third quarter averaged 85kt/d vs a design rate of 98kt/d.   A temporary pre-crushing circuit is being utilised whilst an engineering study to increase capacity of the grinding line is underway.  Ongoing plant optimisation efforts also include two additional tailings thickeners to be installed during 2013.  Antofagasta also announced that it is engaged in a pre-feasibility study into the potential development of the nearby Esperanza Sur deposit (formerly known as Telegrafo) that could potentially produce up to 160kt/a of copper in concentrate from 2018.

**Low head grade hits Batu Hijau** Total consolidated production for the Batu Hijau mine in Indonesia as reported by Newmont amounted to 124Mlbs (56kt) for the year to September, compared to 223Mlb (101kt) over the same period in 2011.  The large fall reflects the fact that the average head grade for the period was just 0.36% Cu compared to 0.57% in the first nine months of 2011.  Mill recovery was lower than in 2011, averaging 67% over the period compared to 78% in 2011.  The mine is currently processing low grade stockpiles as waste stripping continues in an area of the mine known as Phase 6.  Production is forecast to start picking up in 2014 when higher grade ore in this area will be accessed. 

**Padcal production remains suspended** Production from Philex Mining Corporation’s Padcal mine is now not expected to resume before Q2 2013 following a tailings dam leak in August.  The company has allotted 1.06Bn Philippine Peso ($25M) for rehabilitation work and continues to contest a 1.034Bn Philippine Peso fine imposed by the country’s Department of Environment and Nature in connection with the incident.  At full capacity the mine produces 20kt/a of copper in concentrate for export primarily to Japanese smelters. 

**Paranapanema expansion** Production at the Dias d’Avila refinery in Brazil operated by Paranapanema restarted during Q3 following work to increase capacity at the facility to 280kt/a by 2014.  Cathode sales reported by the company for the first nine months of the year were 36.1kt, down by 43% on the equivalent period during 2011.  However overall sales including rods, drawn wire and alloyed products totalled 175.4kt for the period down by just 5.5% on 2011, reflecting increased use of scrap while the ref

inery was out of action. 

**Boschekul equipment order** FLSmidth announced that Kazakhmys had awarded the company a $63M contract for the design and supply of process equipment for the Boschekul project in northern Kazakhstan.  It is understood that that following this order the design throughput of the $1.9Bn project will increase to 30Mt/a (82kt/d) with average production of 100kt/a of copper in concentrate over the first 15 years of the mines operation. 

**Oyu Tolgoi power deal** Turquoise Hill resources announced that Oyu Tolgoi LLC had signed a binding agreement with the Inner Mongolia Power Corporation regarding the supply of electrical power to the Oyu Tolgoi project in Mongolia.  A commissioning programme scheduled for seven weeks is now expected to start imminently with first concentrate production following within a month and the start of commercial production three to five months thereafter.  Under the terms of the Oyu Tolgoi investment agreement, which took effect in 2010, the mine has the right to obtain electrical power from inside or outside Mongolia for up to the first four years of commercial production.  Beyond that period power must be sourced from within Mongolia, with Turquoise Hill having the right to build or sub-contract construction of a coalfired power plant.

**Roseby milestone** Altona Mining announced that it had been granted the final three of the five mining leases that encompass the Roseby copper project, thereby completing the permitting process for the mine.  In September Altona announced that it had received notice from Xstrata Copper that it intended to exercise an option to acquire a 51% interest in Roseby and that an independent valuer had been appointed to determine a fair market price for the transaction.  The deposits that make up the Roseby project are in Queensland around 100km from Mount Isa. Production is forecast to be 39kt/a of copper in concentrate. 

**Fresh uncertainty in DRC** Reports that the town of Goma in the eastern part of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) had fallen to rebels has prompted concerns about more widespread conflict in the central African country. Although the country’s copper producers are located in Katanga province, more than 1000km distant from the unrest and are reported to be unaffected as yet, the news creates fresh uncertainty for companies seeking to invest in mining projects in the country.  In July, the DRC government proposed revisions to the country’s mining code which included free carried state participation in mining projects being increased from 5% to 35%, an increase in royalties payable on base metal production from 2% to 4% of revenue, exploration permits being reduced from five to three years, mining licences being reduced from 30 to 25 years, the scrapping of duty free status on equipment imports and the imposition of a windfall tax.  DRC production of mined copper for 2012 is forecast to be 645kt or around 4% of the global total, with the most significant contributors being Glencore’s operations at Mutanda, Kansuki, Kamoto and KOV together with Freeport McMoRan’s Tenke Fungurume mine.  Sizeable growth potential in the country includes ENRC’s plans to restart the Frontier mine and develop the Kolwezi Tailings project and, in the longer term, Ivanplats’ Kamoa project .
